what: Waste Management collects rubbish and recycling in North America and owns the landfills it goes into. It also captures gas from those landfills and sells it as renewable energy, and has moved into medical waste.
customers: Households through municipal contracts, plus commercial, industrial and healthcare customers.
money: residential, commercial and industrial waste collection
disposal fees at landfills it owns
sorted recyclables and gas captured from landfills
moat: Landfill permits are almost impossible to obtain, so owning disposal capacity near cities is a durable advantage that collection rivals must pay to use.
risks: Volumes follow construction and industrial activity
Debt rose to about $23 billion after the Stericycle acquisition
Recycled commodity prices swing and affect that segment's profit
Fuel and labour costs rise faster than contracted price increases at times
opportunities: Prices rise with inflation under most municipal contracts, protecting margins
Renewable natural gas projects turn a waste product into high-margin energy revenue
Integrating Stericycle adds medical waste, a regulated and higher-priced service
watch: Core price increases against volume, and the ramp-up of renewable natural gas plants.
